paras: The attempted lynching of Johnson at Kaufman, Texas, took place on May 26, 1903, when a mob tried to take a wounded Black prisoner from the Kaufman County jail in order to burn him. Johnson, accused of assaulting a white farmer's wife, was guarded by the sheriff and by militia. He was tried on May 29 and hanged in public the next day, a speed that several Northern papers and a Black weekly called "railroading."

According to a Kaufman report in the Waxahachie Daily Light, Johnson, named there as John Johnson, had lived for a few weeks in a cabin on the Mason farm near Kemp. On Monday, May 25, he was accused of assaulting Mrs. Charles Whitworth, a farmer's wife, after asking her for a drink of water while she was alone; reports through the week called her condition critical.

Accounts of the capture differ. The Waxahachie paper said a posse of neighbors overtook Johnson near Kemp that evening and shot him several times in a running fight; Sheriff Bill Henderson jailed him the next morning. A Dallas dispatch to the St. Louis Republic instead said the sheriff's posse caught him ahead of the mob and shot him when he tried to escape.

On the afternoon of May 26 a mob formed in Kaufman "with the avowed purpose of burning" the prisoner, and Governor Lanham ordered militia companies from Terrell and Dallas to the town. Major E. H. Roach left Dallas by special train with sixty-five men of Company E while the wires to Kaufman were cut. That night Sheriff Henderson, District Judge Dillard and deputies held the jail against the mob, and the troops arrived at 11:40 p.m. The Waxahachie report added that the mob hauled wood to the courthouse square to burn Johnson but "were prevailed upon not to do so," and that the soldiers were ordered back once the excitement subsided.

Johnson was tried on May 29 in what the wire called a "very brief" trial and was sentenced to death. When Judge Dillard asked whether execution should not follow at once, Johnson asked for a single day, and the hanging was set for May 30. A New Orleans dispatch in the New York Sun said he had confessed and waived his appeal and the thirty days the law allowed, and that he was hanged in public for lack of time to build a gallows in the jail. Thousands watched while militia in the railroad yard kept the crowd back, and the Sun reported "no attempt at violence."
No report of any member of the mob being arrested or charged appears in the coverage.

The Associated Press report of the mob and the troops ran from Arizona to Georgia on May 27 and 28 under headlines such as "Threatened with Cremation" and "Troops to Guard Negro." The Waxahachie Daily Light headlined its account "Wanted to Burn" and called Johnson "the criminal" before any trial. The Fredericksburg Free Lance held the case up as one of "white men protecting a colored felon" in Texas.

After the hanging, the New York Sun headlined "Railroaded to His Death" and described "the Nacogdoches way" of immediate execution as popular in Texas because it was said to prevent lynching. The New York World, reprinted in the Birmingham Age-Herald, asked under what "persuasion or compulsion" Johnson had waived his rights, though it judged a "railroaded" penalty less harmful than a lynching. The Buffalo Express, quoted in the Minneapolis Journal, wrote that the case looked "a little too much like the adoption of mob methods by the courts."

The only Black-press item found, in the St. Paul Appeal of June 6, said Kaufman had "railroaded an Afro-American through the courts" and called the hanging "a little improvement upon lynching." The same issue carried a digest line, also printed in the Osceola Times, that Henry Johnson was "legally hanged" within a week of the crime.

The accused is called John Johnson in the Waxahachie report and Henry Johnson in the Sun, the World and the news digests. The Sun named the woman "Mrs. Wentworth," other reports Whitworth; the Republic placed the assault near Ashworth, the Waxahachie paper near Kemp.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Johnson at Kaufman, Texas
bases: A mob tried to take an accused Black man from the Kaufman jail to lynch or burn him and was held off by officers and militia; he was later legally tried and hanged (A1, A2, A3, A13).

The mob that sought to burn Johnson did not reach him (A1, A2); he died by a court-ordered execution after a one-day trial (A10, A13), which papers criticized as 'railroaded' but which was not an extralegal killing by a group (A16, A17).

The Associated Press wire (A3), a St. Louis Republic special from Dallas (A1) and a Kaufman report in the Waxahachie Daily Light (A2) independently report the mob and the militia; the trial and hanging are reported by a separate wire (A10) and a New Orleans dispatch (A13).

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Two militia companies from Terrell and Dallas were ordered to Kaufman after a mob formed to burn the prisoner.

accounts.label: Dallas special (St. Louis Republic)
accounts.gist: The sheriff's posse, not the chasing mob, caught Johnson; he was shot when he tried to escape; that night the mob tried to get him out of jail while wires were cut.

accounts.label: Kaufman report (Waxahachie Daily Light)
accounts.gist: A posse of neighbors shot Johnson several times in a running fight; the sheriff jailed him the next morning; a mob hauled wood to burn him but was talked out of it, and the troops were ordered back.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: Johnson confessed, waived appeal and grace period, and was hanged in public before thousands; only the militia prevented a lynching.

accounts.label: Black editorial (St. Paul Appeal)
accounts.gist: A man 'railroaded' to the gallows in four days, a small improvement over lynching.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'Threatened with Cremation' and 'Troops to Guard Negro' presented the militia call as the story and called Johnson 'the negro.'
The Waxahachie Daily Light headlined 'Wanted to Burn' and called Johnson 'the criminal' before trial, describing citizens who 'unceremoniously fired on' him.
The Free Lance praised white men in Texas for 'protecting a colored felon' from a mob.
The New York Sun ('Railroaded to His Death'), the New York World and the Buffalo Express questioned the speed, the waivers and the public hanging while ranking it above lynching.
The St. Paul Appeal called it railroading 'an Afro-American through the courts', with ironic thanks that it was an improvement on lynching.

conflicts.note: The Waxahachie report is the nearest to Kaufman; the Henry version comes from a New Orleans dispatch and Northern editorials.
Most reports, including the Texas ones, give Whitworth.
Both place the assault in Kaufman County.
